kaigo-atomic-accessible-talk.heading: Support conversation according to communication difficulties
paragraphs: To support communication, check which information the person finds hard to receive and which methods make expressing wishes easier. Do not choose a method from a disease or disability name alone. Ask about experience and preferences, and check whether the method actually works.

When approaching someone with reduced vision, first call their name and give your own name and role. Touching silently can startle them. Describe shapes, features, directions and distances specifically rather than saying only “here” or “there.”

Agree on the reference point for directions. Use the person’s left and right or another agreed reference, such as the direction of a voice, rather than a reference only staff understand. If the person wishes and the object is safe to touch, they can also check it by touch.

Clock positioning describes object directions using clock-face positions. Braille conveys written information, while tactile paving provides mobility cues. These serve different purposes; not every person with reduced vision reads Braille.

For someone with reduced hearing, speak from the front in as quiet a place as possible, with your face and mouth visible. Speak slowly and clearly at a volume suited to them rather than shouting from the start. If a better-hearing side is established, consider it together with visibility of your face.

Written conversation, text-display devices, lipreading, sign language and hearing aids use different routes. Sign language combines not only hands and fingers but facial expressions and head or neck movements to convey meaning. Check which language and methods the person can use.

A hearing aid receives sound through a microphone, processes and amplifies it, and delivers it to the ear. Louder sound alone does not guarantee understanding of words. Using text, pictures or other methods too, check whether the intended message actually reached the person.

Difficulty joining conversations because of reduced hearing may bring loneliness or loss for some people, but do not assume everyone feels the same. Ask about feelings and consider accessible participation and necessary psychological support together.

With aphasia, listening comprehension, speaking, reading and writing are not necessarily affected equally. Choose among short, clear sentences, pictures, gestures and easy-to-answer questions. Do not interrupt every small word error; check the intended meaning. If safety-related information is unclear, clarify rather than guess.

When someone with dementia repeats a story or describes something inconsistent with facts, listen to concerns and anxiety. Speak slowly in short phrases and check necessary facts. Avoid both arguing them into submission and affirming unconfirmed content as fact.

Handing over an ICT or other device does not complete communication support. Check with the person whether they can operate it, understand content and express wishes. Discuss uncertainties with the person responsible, and do not proceed with touch or a change of method without consent.

[Learning example] The person misnames a tool but points to the item they want. Rather than making them wait until they say the correct name, confirm the indicated object and their wish. However, do not omit clarification if safe use is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-record-handover.heading: The receiver also checks records and handoffs
paragraphs: Care plans, progress records, handoff notebooks and meetings each help share information. Recording condition, support provided, responses and results gives the next worker a basis for continuing care. Do not write planned support as performed.

Record as promptly as possible with correct dates and times. If the event time differs from the later recording time, distinguish them using the facility method. Do not fill uncertain memories as though they were confirmed facts.

The person’s words, feelings and wishes are subjective information. Staff observations and actual measurements are objective information, including measured blood pressure or temperature and test data shared by healthcare professionals. Identify the source of test data; care workers must not independently diagnose from it. Subjective information is not worthless, and numbers do not justify ignoring the person’s words. Record the sources separately.

Organize when, where, to whom and what happened, how you responded and any known reason. The 5W1H approach helps communicate; it is not a form requiring invented causes. If the cause is unknown, report it as unconfirmed.

Treat names, addresses, phone numbers and photographs as personal information. Through facility procedures, check purpose, necessary scope, recipients, method, consent or other appropriate basis. Do not put personal or workplace accounts on private social media or discuss them outside without authorization.

The sender briefly communicates key points, separating observations from judgments and assumptions. Choose timing according to urgency and, for routine consultation, check a location that prevents information leakage. Share staff work status or observations from contact with the person too when needed for support.

The receiver’s role goes beyond listening. Note necessary details and repeat important points such as times, the person concerned, response, next responsible worker and unknowns to check them. Silence or lack of objection does not prove understanding or acceptance of responsibility.

Making a call, receipt of the message, acceptance of the next task and completed action are separate states. Do not record a problem as resolved merely because contact was made. Confirm who will check what next and how results will be reported.

Consultation means asking colleagues or professionals for opinions or help about uncertainties or problems. Specify what is unclear and ask someone whose role fits. A wish to finish quickly does not justify decisions beyond your responsibilities.

For urgent changes or accidents, immediately seek assistance and make contact rather than waiting to complete a form. This explanation teaches recording and information handling; it does not independently set emergency procedures, legal sharing grounds or medical judgments.

[Learning example] After a report containing several times, the receiver remains silent. Ask them to repeat important times, the person concerned, the next task and unknowns to check shared understanding. Do not record silence as agreement.

kaigo-atomic-continence-types.heading: Distinguish toileting equipment and mechanisms of leakage
paragraphs: A portable commode may be used when reaching the toilet is difficult despite an urge, or at night. Urinals and bedpans support people who have difficulty moving or sitting, among others. Knowing their purpose differs from choosing and setting up suitable equipment. The material also gives bed equipment examples for physically weakened people and shows differently shaped urinals labeled for men or women. Labels alone do not establish fit; check the body, posture and actual product.

Diapers and pads help manage urine or stool leakage or difficulty using a toilet. However, they do not replace investigating causes, toileting opportunities, personal agency or skin observation. Check habits and necessary assistance. Some people also struggle to use a portable commode, so consider methods individually according to condition.

Leakage when coughing or sneezing increases abdominal pressure describes stress urinary incontinence. Distinguish it from urgency incontinence, in which a sudden strong urge results in leakage before reaching the toilet. Do not interpret “urgency” as always meaning psychological tension.

Other mechanisms include overflow incontinence, where retained bladder urine leaks gradually, and reflex leakage related to nerve impairment. Describe leakage accurately, but its appearance alone does not allow care workers to establish type or cause.

Functional incontinence relates to difficulty reaching the toilet, handling clothing or recognizing its location in time. A person may feel an urge but be unable to find the toilet. Check routes, guidance, suitable timing and assistance rather than treating every leak as the same mechanism.

Constipation may relate to bodily functions or obstructed passage caused by tumors, inflammation or other problems. Beyond counting days, compare with usual bowel movements and record amount, frequency, stool condition, distress and changes. Refer to healthcare professionals when the cause requires assessment.

Bowel opportunities matching habits, fluids and fiber consistent with the plan, and permitted activity can support daily life with constipation. Report lack of improvement. Do not uniformly increase fluid or fiber without checking fluid restrictions, swallowing, illness and obstruction. This material does not authorize independent medication changes.

Diarrhea involves repeated watery stools and requires attention to dehydration and irritation around the anus. Report new diarrhea to healthcare professionals, including possible infection concerns. Prevent prolonged stool contact with skin and maintain cleanliness and skin condition using facility methods.

Whether oral fluid replacement is possible, and its type and amount, require checks of swallowing, underlying conditions, healthcare instructions and the plan. Examples of warm water or sports drinks do not mean giving everyone identical amounts. A comfortable drinking temperature alone does not establish suitable replacement for that person.

Listen to discomfort, embarrassment and anxiety around toileting without blame or teasing. Observe urine and stool and communicate health abnormalities according to urgency. Completed cleaning does not complete condition checks. Psychological tension may also affect elimination, so ask about difficulties in a way that encourages sharing.

[Learning example] The person feels an urge but cannot find the toilet in time. Go beyond changing the diaper: check guidance, mobility help, timing, skin and wishes. Do not diagnose a cause from the leakage outcome alone.

kaigo-atomic-toilet-environment.heading: Arrange toileting stages and a usable environment
paragraphs: Toileting includes noticing the urge, reaching the place, arranging clothes and posture, eliminating, cleaning, replacing clothes and leaving. Identify which stages require help and preserve the parts the person can perform.

Easy-to-operate doors such as sliding doors, wheelchair access space, usable grab bars and a reachable call button support toilet use. Check odor, ventilation and privacy too. Installed equipment alone does not establish that the person can use it.

Examples use L-shaped grab bars for support while standing and adjustable bars for approach and bodily needs. A call button requests help when difficulties occur or toileting ends. Check reach and operation with the person in the actual position. The material’s adjustable bar moves up and down; in practice, check the product method and the person’s movements.

In a hemiplegia example, the usable hand holds the bar while the helper supports the weaker side. Before standing, check foot position, clothes and the holding point separately. Do not substitute pulling the paralyzed arm to stand the person. The source example lowers pants and underwear while the unaffected hand holds the bar and the affected side is supported, then uses the bar to sit. Do not apply this flow to everyone; use an individual method with standing and transfer ability confirmed.

Check stable sitting. Adjusting clothing while seated within the person’s ability reduces tasks performed standing. Support standing only when possible and permitted, using the planned method. After standing, check stability and whether clothing is arranged.

Discuss wishes to be alone together with calling methods and necessary observation. Closing a door or staff leaving depends on wishes and assessed risk. An illustration of a worker leaving does not instruct staff to leave everyone alone.

For a portable commode, check position, seat, stability and necessary support against individual needs. After use, manage cleanliness, clothing, hand hygiene, odor and equipment, and support return to a safe place.

For a bedpan, prepare supplies, privacy screening, body coverings and waterproof protection, and confirm planned posture and suitable working height. Ask for hip lifting only when possible and permitted. Check bedpan stability, position and absence of skin pressure. The material shows someone able to bend knees and lift hips while clothes are lowered and the pan inserted. Align the anus with the receiving area and cover the body to reduce exposure. Do not demand difficult hip or knee movements; use a permitted, trained method.

The raised-back bedpan example explains a posture that facilitates abdominal pressure. It does not tell everyone to strain hard; actual bed elevation follows condition and plan. Urinals differ in shape. Source examples support the back with a pillow in side-lying or use paper to direct urine into the urinal. Confirm a trained method suited to the body, repositioning ability and actual product. Check placement, leakage, splashing and skin contact; sex labels do not guarantee one shape fits.

After use, clean according to facility methods and remove the pan in a way suited to the person. The material shows an able person lifting their hips for removal, followed by skin observation and side-lying to remove waterproof sheets. Confirm permitted hip lifting or repositioning methods. Arrange clothes and bedding, return the bed to a safe height, check condition and feelings, then process supplies. Removal of the pan alone is not completion.

For toileting assistance, choose gloves, aprons and other protection according to anticipated blood, body-fluid or excreta contact and facility procedures. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Perform required changes and hygiene when moving from dirty to clean work. The material gives a disposable-apron example; use, replacement and disposal follow facility infection precautions and product instructions.

This lesson organizes purposes and checks of assistance. Transfers, repositioning and equipment handling follow the individual plan and practical training. If instability, pain, abnormal skin or changed condition appears, do not force continuation. Arrange necessary help and reporting.

[Learning example] When seated on the toilet, the person cannot reach a call button behind their back. Check actual seated reach and operation with them, beyond whether a button is present. Also review grab bars, approach routes, observation and privacy.

kaigo-atomic-clothing-seated.heading: Check balance during seated dressing
paragraphs: First ask about condition and desired clothes, explain the purpose and assistance and confirm consent. Provide privacy and suitable room temperature. For reduced vision, explain clothing shape and features and offer touch if wanted.

A hemiplegic dressing principle is to undress the unaffected side first and dress the paralyzed side first. Removing the easier-moving side first reduces movement demands on the weaker side. However, memorized order must not override individual pain or movement restrictions.

Check sitting stability and the side toward which balance may be lost. In the seated hemiplegia example, weaker force on the paralyzed side makes falling that way more likely, so the worker supports that side. Choose actual support from individual assessment; do not generalize this position to every person or posture. Help with difficult reaches or sleeves rather than pulling the shoulder or paralyzed arm hard.

Raising a foot to change pants may upset balance. Use reliable support when standing is possible and permitted. For unstable standing, the material also shows the person remaining seated, lifting the unaffected hip and lowering pants as far as possible. Check whether that movement is possible and permitted. Do not force hip lifting, foot lifting or standing on someone leaning unstably. Review support and method if difficult and choose help matching the plan.

The pants-dressing example also threads the paralyzed leg first, then the unaffected leg. Pull pants up as far as possible seated, then adjust standing only if necessary and safe. Do not confuse the unaffected-first undressing, affected-first dressing principle with a requirement to stand.

Afterward, check underwear and fabric creases, displacement, comfort, pain, skin and condition. Clothing being on the body does not establish safe, comfortable dressing. Actual methods follow the person’s plan and training.

[Learning example] During a pants change, the person is leaning while seated, but staff ask them to raise a foot. Stop the destabilizing method, check condition, support and possible postures, and seek necessary help.

kaigo-atomic-clothing-bed.heading: Dressing in bed and checks afterward
paragraphs: In bed-based hemiplegic dressing too, check what the person can do and use unaffected-side-first undressing and paralyzed-side-first dressing. Before starting, arrange checks of condition, explanation and consent, room temperature, privacy and clothing choice.

The top-removal example takes off the unaffected sleeve first and gathers the removed fabric inward. Use safe repositioning suited to the person when moving clothes from under the body. Do not forcefully pull the body or paralyzed shoulder to remove fabric.

The textbook example turns the person onto the unaffected side, removes fabric from the back and then removes the paralyzed sleeve. This direction may not suit every illness or injury. Confirm permitted positions, shoulder protection, staffing and equipment through assessment and training.

For dressing, the example threads the paralyzed sleeve, arranges the body of the garment, spreads the back through planned repositioning and threads the unaffected sleeve. Check back and side seam positions, creases and twists. Putting clothes on differs from checking comfort.

Pants too are removed from the unaffected side first and put on the paralyzed side first in the example. An illustration of someone able to lift their hips does not require everyone to do so. Check possibility and permission; use an individual assistance method when it is not feasible.

Helper positions need not match between seated and lying dressing. The lying top example approaches from the unaffected side to handle buttons and gather clothes. Seated stability involves different conditions. Do not mechanically apply one position to every action.

Afterward, ask how the person feels and check pain, skin, clothing position, fabric creases and condition. Correct twisted seams in a safe position. Do not finish with comfort problems unresolved merely because the appearance or operation is complete.
[Learning example] The top is on, but the back seam is twisted. Adjust it in a safe position and check pain, comfort and skin. Do not conclude “dressed, therefore finished.”

kaigo-atomic-face-hair-makeup.heading: Support face washing, hair and makeup through personal choice
paragraphs: Face washing removes skin dirt and helps start the day comfortably. If independent washing is difficult, check wishes and condition and assist needed areas with a suitable towel or other method.
Even with a warm towel, check temperature and tolerance. Removing dirt differs from moisturizing to prevent dryness. Choose methods and products suited to skin rather than one product for everyone.

Ask hairstyle preferences and check hair and scalp before arranging it. Someone with difficulty raising an arm may still manage parts using a comb with a suitable handle or shape. Do not finish at handing over equipment; check posture and ease of use.

The material explains that scalp brushing removes dirt and appropriate stimulation promotes circulation. It does not mean increasing force or rubbing continuously. Avoid pain or skin strain, and discuss the desired style and necessary help. A request to arrange hair is not permission for an unwanted hairstyle change.

Makeup is one way to express individuality. Support those who want it and do not force those who do not. Before bed, support removal using skin-appropriate methods while retaining the parts the person can do.

This explanation teaches choice and checking points. Review methods and consult the necessary person if skin abnormalities or pain occur. It does not instruct staff to substitute cosmetics or moisturizers for treatment of skin disease.

[Learning example] The person wants to comb their hair but has difficulty raising an arm. Check preferred hairstyle and scalp condition, discuss equipment and posture adjustments and let them perform possible parts with help for difficult parts.

127.title: Support conversation according to communication difficulties
objectives: Choose methods suited to vision, hearing, understanding and expression.
Separate minor word errors from information requiring safety checks.
127.context: [Learning example] The person misnames a tool but points to the item they want. Rather than making them wait until they say the correct name, confirm the indicated object and their wish. However, do not omit clarification if safe use is unclear.
127.artCaption: Use pictures and pointing to check together what the person wants to convey.

128.title: The receiver also checks records and handoffs
objectives: Record subjective and objective information, sources and event times separately.
The receiver repeats key points, distinguishing acceptance of a task from completion.
128.context: [Learning example] After a report containing several times, the receiver remains silent. Ask them to repeat important times, the person concerned, the next task and unknowns to check shared understanding. Do not record silence as agreement.
128.artCaption: Staff hand over information. The receiver also checks key points and the next responsible worker.

129.title: Distinguish toileting equipment and mechanisms of leakage
objectives: Distinguish equipment purposes and different urinary-incontinence mechanisms.
Link constipation and diarrhea support with the person’s plan, observations and reporting.
129.context: [Learning example] The person feels an urge but cannot find the toilet in time. Go beyond changing the diaper: check guidance, mobility help, timing, skin and wishes. Do not diagnose a cause from the leakage outcome alone.
129.artCaption: Consider toileting-equipment purposes and individual conditions. The image is not a procedure for selecting or installing equipment.

130.title: Arrange toileting stages and a usable environment
objectives: Identify needed assistance at each toileting stage.
Check calling, grab bars, privacy and cleanliness under actual use conditions.
130.context: [Learning example] When seated on the toilet, the person cannot reach a call button behind their back. Check actual seated reach and operation with them, beyond whether a button is present. Also review grab bars, approach routes, observation and privacy.
130.artCaption: Check the toilet environment, including whether grab bars and calling can be used in the person’s actual posture.

131.title: Check balance during seated dressing
objectives: Check clothing choices and consent to help.
Check sitting stability and comfort rather than relying only on dressing order.
131.context: [Learning example] During a pants change, the person is leaning while seated, but staff ask them to raise a foot. Stop the destabilizing method, check condition, support and possible postures, and seek necessary help.
131.artCaption: The person chooses desired clothing. Needing assistance does not transfer clothing choices to staff.

132.title: Dressing in bed and checks afterward
objectives: Distinguish lying-dressing examples from individual posture conditions.
Finish after checking twisted seams, pain, skin and comfort.
132.context: [Learning example] The top is on, but the back seam is twisted. Adjust it in a safe position and check pain, comfort and skin. Do not conclude “dressed, therefore finished.”
132.artCaption: Listen to wishes near the bed. The picture does not illustrate a technical procedure for changing clothes while lying.

133.title: Support face washing, hair and makeup through personal choice
objectives: Adjust equipment and posture to use retained abilities.
133.context: [Learning example] The person wants to comb their hair but has difficulty raising an arm. Check preferred hairstyle and scalp condition, discuss equipment and posture adjustments and let them perform possible parts with help for difficult parts.
133.artCaption: Support personal choices and possible actions. This is not a diagram of face washing, hair arranging or cosmetic use.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-accessible-talk.prompt: The person misnames a tool but points to what they want. Which response is appropriate?
options: Withhold checking wishes and assistance until they say the correct name.
Confirm the indicated item and wish, clarify safety uncertainties and arrange necessary help.
Incorrect pronunciation proves all understanding is lost.
Identifying the pointed-at item confirms intended use and wishes too.
rationales: This makes correcting a minor word error a condition for communicating intent.
This respects intended meaning without inventing safety information.
Pronunciation or expression difficulty alone cannot determine comprehension.
Identifying an object does not establish purpose or safety conditions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-record-handover.prompt: After a handoff containing several times, the receiver stays silent. How should understanding be checked?
options: Ask the receiver to repeat key times, the person concerned, next actions and unknowns, then check for misunderstandings.
Record full understanding and completed actions because there was no objection.
Remove all times because they are complicated.
Refuse questions because the message was already sent.
rationales: Have the receiver repeat content rather than only repeating your own explanation. Silence is not evidence of understanding or task acceptance.
Understanding, acceptance and completed performance each require checking.
Removing times loses the course of events and deadlines for next actions.
Two-way checking of uncertainties is needed; one transmission is insufficient.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-continence-type.prompt: The person feels an urge but cannot find the toilet in time. Which support is appropriate?
options: After leakage, urge or mobility difficulties need no checking.
A diaper change removes checks of skin and wishes.
Check causes, surroundings, guidance and timing while protecting agency, skin and privacy.
Treat every urine leak as the same mechanism.
rationales: The person has an urge, so check location and mobility factors behind delay.
Changing alone does not establish skin condition or preferred toileting method.
Location or movement difficulties may prevent timely toileting despite an urge; managing leakage alone is insufficient.
Distinguish abdominal pressure, urgency, retained urine, nerve and daily-activity mechanisms.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-toilet-environm.prompt: The call button is behind the person when seated on the toilet and is out of reach. What should be checked?
options: Its presence is sufficient; leave position unchanged.
Check reach and operation in the actual seated posture, reviewing bars, approach and privacy too.
Always leave the door open without asking because calling is impossible.
Grab bars remove the need for calling.
rationales: Installation alone does not establish access to help.
Checking actual use creates an environment in which needed help can be requested.
Adjust privacy and safety according to wishes and observation needs.
Grab bars support posture; calling requests assistance.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-clothing-seated.prompt: During a pants change, staff ask the leaning seated person to lift a foot. What should be reviewed?
options: Correct undressing order removes balance checks.
Changing quickly permits continued instability.
Everyone seated can lift a foot.
Stop the destabilizing method, check condition, support and possible postures, and preserve choice and privacy.
rationales: Affected/unaffected order alone does not guarantee seated stability.
Saving time does not justify a method risking falls.
Raising a foot can disturb balance even while seated; check ability and support.
Adjust to personal abilities rather than turning an order into compulsory standing.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-clothing-bed.prompt: The top is on, but the back seam is twisted. What is appropriate?
options: Sleeves being on removes comfort checks.
An unseen back seam does not affect the person.
Correct the twist in a safe position and check skin, pain and comfort with the person.
Pull fabric hard without checking posture or pain.
rationales: Completed handling alone does not establish pain or skin strain.
Back twists and creases can cause discomfort or skin strain.
This distinguishes putting clothes on from safe, comfortable arrangement.
Adjusting fabric still requires checks of safe posture and bodily strain.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-face-hair-makeu.prompt: The person wants to comb their hair but cannot easily raise an arm. Which support is appropriate?
options: Check preferred style and scalp, discuss suitable tools and posture and preserve possible actions.
Difficulty raising an arm transfers hairstyle choice to staff.
Hand over a comb without checking actual use.
Rub the scalp hard despite pain to improve circulation.
rationales: Equipment and posture can preserve ability with help only for difficult parts, rather than complete takeover.
Needing physical help does not remove the right to choose.
Equipment presence does not establish usability with personal posture and ability.
Do not make stronger stimulation the goal; avoid pain and skin strain.
